scenes.heading: Errors you will meet, and what to do

cards.title: Fix the request
cards.body: Bad parameters or an unknown model. Retrying won't help.

cards.title: Fix the key
cards.body: Missing, wrong or under-privileged API key.

cards.title: Slow down
cards.body: Rate limit reached. Wait, then retry.

cards.title: Retry later
cards.body: A server problem or overload, often temporary.

cards.title: Check the connection
cards.body: No response at all, or a timeout.

scenes.question: Which error should your code retry?
scenes.explain: A 429 recovers after waiting. 400, 401 and 404 fail the same way every time until you fix the request or the key.

items.text: 4xx (except 429): fix the request or the key; don't retry
429, 5xx, network: retry with backoff; the SDK does it for you
Cost = tokens × price; count, track and budget

captions.text: A demo that works once is easy.
A program that keeps working when the network drops, when you hit a rate limit, or
when costs start to climb, takes deliberate design.
This lesson covers the production basics every AI application needs.
You'll recognise the API's error types, and know what to do about each one.
Catch errors in the right order.
Understand rate limits, and the SDK's automatic retries.
And calculate and control what each call costs.
Errors fall into groups.
A four hundred or four oh four means your request is wrong: a bad parameter, or a
model name that doesn't exist.
Retrying won't help.
Fix the request.
Four oh one and four oh three are about your key: missing, wrong, or without
permission.
Again, don't retry.
Fix the key.
Four twenty-nine means you've hit a rate limit.
Waiting and retrying is exactly right.
Five hundreds, including five twenty-nine for overloaded, are server-side problems
that are often temporary.
Retry after a short wait.
And connection errors and timeouts mean no proper response came back at all.
Those are also worth a retry.
The rule is simple: retry rate limits, server errors, and network problems.
Never blindly retry the other four hundreds.
For this demo only, we turn off automatic retries, so every error reaches our code.
The call goes inside a try block.
Then we catch specific exception classes, most specific first: an authentication
error, then a rate limit error.
API status error is the parent class of every HTTP error, so it catches anything we
haven't handled, and gives us the status code.
Connection errors aren't HTTP errors at all, so they have their own class.
If you catch the parent first, the specific handlers never run.
To demonstrate errors without breaking anything, the fake API reads an environment
variable telling it how to fail.
With no failure, a normal placeholder reply.
A four oh one becomes, check your API key.
A four twenty-nine becomes, rate limited.
And a five twenty-nine, an overloaded server, falls through to the general status
handler.
Every API account has rate limits: how many requests and tokens you may use per
minute.
When you exceed them, you get a four twenty-nine.
The standard response is to retry with exponential backoff.
Wait a short time, plus a little randomness so that many clients don't all retry at
the same moment, and try again.
If it fails again, wait roughly twice as long.
Good news: the Anthropic SDK already does all of this for you.
It retries rate limits, server errors, and connection errors twice by default, with
backoff, and it respects the retry after header the API sends.
You control this with max retries, on the client or per request.
Two is the default, and zero turns it off.
Here the fake API fails with a four twenty-nine and then a five hundred.
Setting ANTHROPIC LOG to info shows what the SDK does: it waits about half a second,
retries, waits about a second, retries again, and succeeds.
Our code didn't need a single extra line.
Set a timeout you're comfortable with.
The SDK default is ten minutes.
For long replies, stream instead of waiting.
When something fails, log the request ID.
It identifies exactly which request went wrong.
Use separate keys for separate apps and environments, so you can revoke one without
breaking the others.
And never send keys to the model, or print them in logs.
Logs are often far less protected than you think.
Now, money.
You pay per token, with separate prices for input and output, quoted per million
tokens.
Claude Opus 5.5, the most capable of the three and our default, costs four dollars
per million input tokens, and twenty per million output tokens.
Sonnet 5.5 costs half that.
And Haiku 5.5 is far cheaper, for simple, high-volume work.
These are list prices in October 2026.
Prices change, so always check the official pricing page.
And notice that output tokens cost five times more than input tokens.
Here's the cost calculation.
Prices are per million tokens.
Count tokens measures a request before you send it, so you can warn about, or block,
a request that would be too big or too expensive.
After the call, usage gives the actual tokens.
Multiply each by its price, and divide by a million.
And then the important habit: multiply by your expected traffic.
A fraction of a cent per call.
But the same call ten thousand times a day costs real money every day.
In offline mode these token counts are rough estimates.
With a real key, they're exact.
Five ways to control cost.
First, send less: trim history, and include only relevant documents.
Second, ask for concise answers, with a sensible max tokens.
Third, use lower effort for simple tasks.
Fourth, pick the smallest model that does the job well, measured on real examples,
not guessed.
And fifth, track spending in code, with a budget that stops runaway loops.
Our project does exactly this.
Quick check.
Which of these errors should your code retry?
The four twenty-nine.
A rate limit recovers after waiting.
The others fail the same way every time, until you fix the request or the key.
Four hundreds, except four twenty-nine, need a fix, not a retry.
Rate limits, server errors, and network errors are retried with backoff, and the SDK
does that for you.
Catch specific exception classes before the general one.
And cost is tokens times price, so count, track, and budget.
You now know everything the project needs.
